title: The long way home
description: A shoreline, a detour, and six seconds of quiet.
text: I left the house with a plan to get somewhere. By the water, the plan felt less interesting than the way there. The tide had drawn a new line across the sand. Someone had left a very small stack of stones. Beyond the bend, the path disappeared into the trees. A walk in three frames A rust-coloured sun hangs above a green shoreline. A slow drift along the illustrated shoreline A winding path crosses layers of green hills. The film is six seconds long and silent. That is about how long I stood still before deciding to keep walking. Some days, the detour is the part you came for. What came back with me Not much: a sentence, an idea for a drawing, and the sense that the afternoon had become a little larger. I put the pictures in Daylight . If you want an excuse for your own detour, take the field guide . Sample story and original illustrations. No real journey is being documented.

title: A desk with room
description: An open notebook, one useful question, and a little less clutter.
text: I cleared the desk until only three things remained: a notebook, a pencil, and a cup. The cup was mostly an excuse to sit down. An open notebook, pencil, and coffee on a warm wooden desk. The empty space did not make the work easier. It made the next thing easier to see. One useful question Before starting, I wrote: What would make today feel complete? Not impressive. Complete. Keep Put aside One small task A list of twenty A rough first pass The perfect opening A ten-minute window Waiting for a free day By lunch there was a paragraph on the page. It was not the paragraph I expected, which was a good sign. A quiet minute A slow shoreline study, six seconds without sound This tiny film sits in the middle of the story because words sometimes need an interval. Clear a little space. Write the first sentence. Come back tomorrow. If a blank document feels too formal, try the writing room . Ten minutes is plenty for a beginning.

title: Four studies in light
description: The same small palette, four different afternoons.
text: These drawings began as a rule: four colours, a few shapes, and no detail that did not earn its place. Warm light falls across a tall arched window. A notebook and coffee sit in a diagonal band of sunlight. A terracotta sun glows above the shoreline. A light path runs between dark green hills. The window feels still. The desk feels expectant. The shore seems to be leaving. The path seems to be arriving. What changed The palette stayed nearly the same. The amount of empty space did not. Leaving more room around a shape made it feel less like an object and more like a place. You can switch the collection to Spotlight to spend a moment with each drawing. The same images live in the gallery . Original sample illustrations, drawn for this site.

title: An afternoon at the movies
description: A little space for someone else’s imagination.
text: A personal journal can have a screening room, too. This one has a single seat and no programme to keep up with. Big Buck Bunny — Blender Foundation short film The player loads only when you choose to play it. The film stays with its original publisher. After the credits Write down one image you remember. Not a review, not a verdict. Just an image. Mine would go beside the drawings in Daylight , or in the writing room while it is still fresh. Film credit: Blender Foundation / Big Buck Bunny . Linked here as a sample external video.

title: A place to begin
description: Sample entry: on making a small space for ideas, without needing to know where they lead.
text: This is sample content. Edit it in the browser editor, unpublish it, or remove its Markdown file from the repository. There is something useful about a blank page. It asks very little: a thought, a sentence, perhaps an observation from the walk home. This journal is a place to collect those things. Not everything needs to become a project. Sometimes it is enough to notice, and to write it down. Making a little room The internet can feel like a place where everything has to be finished. A personal site offers a different possibility. You can leave a question open. You can return to an idea months later. Start with what you noticed. The rest can follow. For now, the plan is simple: Write when there is something worth remembering. Keep the pages comfortable to read. Let the collection grow at its own pace. If you are curious about the person behind these notes, there is an about page .

title: The value of small things
description: Sample entry: a notebook, an afternoon walk, and the quiet satisfaction of paying attention.
text: This is sample content, included to show how a second journal entry looks. Some of the most useful things I own are also the simplest. A notebook that fits in a pocket. A mug with a comfortable handle. A list of books I might read one day. Their value is in how often I return to them. A small experiment For a week, I tried writing down one thing each day that I would otherwise forget. Nothing dramatic: the light on a wall, a good sentence, the name of a tree. By Sunday I had seven small reasons to pay more attention. The point was not to turn the habit into a system. It was to make a little more of the day visible.

text: This is a sample page. Replace it with your own introduction. Hello, I’m Your name . This is where I write about the things I make, the things I learn, and the details I want to remember. title: Daylight
description: A collection of drawings and a small film.
text: Some things belong together before there is a story to connect them. These are mine for now. Afternoon light through an arched window. A notebook waiting on a sunlit desk. Six seconds by the illustrated shore A path through overlapping green hills. A loose collection Use Grid to see the collection together, or Spotlight to move through it one piece at a time. The gallery has everything, with tags to narrow the view. Four studies in light tells the story behind the palette.

title: A small field guide
description: Three printable pages for a slower afternoon.
text: Page 1 — A small field guide Stupid Simple Blogging · Sample edition Three pages for a slower afternoon. No destination required. An illustrated shoreline: green waves and a sandy coast beneath a warm orange sun. Take a short walk. Notice one thing you would usually pass. Bring back a sentence, a shape, or a question. Print it, keep it on your phone, or leave it open beside a notebook. A little room for noticing. Page 2 — Leave the route a little open Out there. Fifteen minutes is enough. So is the view from a window. Look for a line. The edge of a shadow. A branch against the sky. A path that bends out of sight. Wait for a change. Stay with the view for a minute. What moves? What stays? What did you miss at first? Keep one detail. Write a sentence. Draw a shape. Record a few quiet seconds. One thing is enough. There is no right thing to come back with. Leave places as you found them. The smallest observation can make a good story. Page 3 — Keep a little of it Back here. The printable page leaves blank space for a date, a place, and these four prompts. You can also answer them in your own notebook or text editor: One thing I noticed A colour, sound, or shape The sentence I want to keep Something to return to An original sample booklet for Stupid Simple Blogging. Made to be printed, scribbled on, and changed. Until the next small detour.

title: A little layout studio
description: Rows, columns and small HTML tools, with a complete static reading experience.
text: Room for more than a post A page can hold an introduction beside an illustration, then a table beside a useful tool. Each column is ordinary reading content, and every row has a predictable order. On a narrow screen the columns stack. Nothing needs a script to lay out this page. Browse the journal or see the media collection . An illustrated desk with a notebook, plant and cup in soft light. A little space for making things. A few ways to make a page Choose a starting point Format Good for Markdown A flowing article Page builder Rows, columns, images and notes HTML snippet A table, aside or a small interactive tool A small reading-time tool Estimate reading time by dividing the word count by 200 words per minute and rounding up to a whole minute. This is a rough planning aid; people and texts vary. Words Estimated time 200 1 minute 500 3 minutes 1,000 5 minutes The optional calculator below applies that same formula. It requires JavaScript; the explanation and examples above do not. Make this your own Open this page in the editor and choose a column. Write with Markdown, insert media, or add an HTML snippet. Change column widths, move rows, and use Undo if you change your mind. Static HTML belongs to the reading page. Interactive HTML runs in its own frame, alongside an explanation that is available to everyone.

title: Now
description: A small snapshot of what has my attention.
text: A sample now page · October 2026 Making A set of simple illustrations. A journal that feels lived in. Enough room for both words and pictures. Noticing The light arrives at the desk a little later each morning. The notebook still opens to yesterday's page. Coffee and a notebook in the afternoon sun. Trying One short walk without headphones. Ten minutes in the writing room . Printing the field guide and leaving it by the door. Leaving open What should this place become? For now, a useful answer is: somewhere to return to.

title: A small place for good things.
description: Field notes, little experiments, and things worth keeping.
text: An illustrated green shoreline, a warm sun, and a winding band of sand. Welcome in. This is a sample corner of the internet: a journal to read, pictures to linger over, and a few things to try. Start somewhere Take the long way home — a walk told in pictures and a short film. Look at the light — a small collection, with room to browse. Make ten minutes — an uncluttered place to write. Keep a field guide — three printable pages for your next slow afternoon. Three things, lately A window at four. A notebook left open. The line where water meets land. Afternoon light across an arched window and a potted plant. An open notebook and a cup of coffee on a sunlit desk. A pale footpath winds through overlapping green hills. Come back when you like The journal holds the longer stories. Topics connect the loose threads. The gallery gathers the pictures and films in one place. No hurry. There is always another page.
